\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{यदि} (yadi)}{यदि (yadi)}]{\sk{यदि} (yadi) — if}

\label{lesson:SA-C154-yadi}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for all around, then the Sanskrit for on all sides.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{यदि}}
\textbf{\sk{यदि}} — \emph{yadi} — \textquotedblleft{}if\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{yadi} \textquotedblleft{}if\textquotedblright{} is built on the relative stem \emph{ya-} \textquotedblleft{}which\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 10410), already in the Rigveda (MW). MW compares the relative \emph{ya-} with Greek \emph{hos} \textquotedblleft{}who\textquotedblright{}. It lives on as Punjabi \emph{je} and Marathi \emph{jai} \textquotedblleft{}if\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 10410).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{yadi}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Sanskrit for all around, then the Sanskrit for on all sides, then say \emph{yadi} again
\end{itemize}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{चेत्} (cet)}{चेत् (cet)}]{\sk{चेत्} (cet) — provided that, if}

\label{lesson:SA-C154-cet}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for on all sides, then the Sanskrit for if.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{चेत्}}
\textbf{\sk{चेत्}} — \emph{cet} — \textquotedblleft{}provided that, if\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{cet} is \emph{ced}, built from \emph{ca} \textquotedblleft{}and\textquotedblright{} + \emph{id}, an emphatic particle, as the Vedic word-by-word text splits it (MW). It first meant \textquotedblleft{}and\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}when\textquotedblright{}, and later \textquotedblleft{}if\textquotedblright{}; like \emph{ca}, it follows the first word of its clause.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{cet}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{cet}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Sanskrit for on all sides, then the Sanskrit for if, then say \emph{cet} again
\end{itemize}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{तथापि} (tathāpi)}{तथापि (tathāpi)}]{\sk{तथापि} (tathāpi) — even so, still}

Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for if, then the Sanskrit for provided that.

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{तथापि}}
\textbf{\sk{तथापि}} — \emph{tathāpi} — \textquotedblleft{}even so, still\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{tathāpi} is built from \emph{tathā} \textquotedblleft{}so, thus\textquotedblright{}, on the pronoun base \emph{ta-} \textquotedblleft{}that\textquotedblright{}, and \emph{api} \textquotedblleft{}even, also\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 5647): \textquotedblleft{}even so, nevertheless\textquotedblright{}. CDIAL 5647 traces Punjabi \emph{te} \textquotedblleft{}and\textquotedblright{} to it.
\end{cousinweb}

\emph{yadyapi} is built from \emph{yadi} \textquotedblleft{}if\textquotedblright{} and \emph{api} \textquotedblleft{}even, also\textquotedblright{}, with \emph{i} turning to \emph{y} before the vowel (MW): \textquotedblleft{}even if\textquotedblright{}, so \textquotedblleft{}although\textquotedblright{}. It pairs with \emph{tathāpi} \textquotedblleft{}even so\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{अथवा} (athavā)}{अथवा (athavā)}]{\sk{अथवा} (athavā) — or else, or}

\label{lesson:SA-C154-athava}

Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for even so, then the Sanskrit for although.

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{अथवा}}
\textbf{\sk{अथवा}} — \emph{athavā} — \textquotedblleft{}or else, or\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{athavā} is built from \emph{atha} \textquotedblleft{}then, now\textquotedblright{} and \emph{vā} \textquotedblleft{}or\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 231): \textquotedblleft{}or else, or rather\textquotedblright{}. MW compares \emph{vā} with Latin \emph{-ve} \textquotedblleft{}or\textquotedblright{}, which also follows the word it joins.
\end{cousinweb}
